lessons.title: Food microbiology
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus (Upper Sixth part) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe growth of microorganisms and calculate growth
Describe important pathogens and spoilage organisms
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Thresholds (aw 0.9, pH 4.6) are standard guidance values. Pathogen list is an outline; verify against the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Growth
blocks.md: Bacteria multiply by **binary fission**: N = N0 x 2^n, where n = t/g is the number of generations (g = generation time). Growth curve: **lag**, **log**, **stationary**, **death**. Spores of some bacteria (Bacillus, Clostridium) survive boiling and germinate when conditions allow. Yeasts reproduce by budding; moulds by spores and hyphae.

blocks.title: Factors
blocks.md: **Intrinsic** (in the food): water activity (aw: most bacteria need above about 0.9; many moulds grow lower), pH (low-acid foods above about 4.6 allow growth of Clostridium botulinum in sealed, oxygen-free conditions), nutrients, natural antimicrobials, structure. **Extrinsic** (environment): temperature, humidity, atmosphere (oxygen), time.

blocks.caption: Four boxes listing the phases of the bacterial growth curve.
blocks.alt: Flow of phases: lag, log, stationary, death.

blocks.title: Pathogens (outline)
blocks.md: **Salmonella** (poultry, eggs; infection). **Escherichia coli** (some strains; contaminated food/water). **Staphylococcus aureus** (from skin and nose; heat-stable toxin). **Clostridium botulinum** (inadequately canned low-acid foods; very potent toxin). **Bacillus cereus** (rice; toxins). **Listeria** (can grow in the fridge). **Vibrio cholerae** and **Salmonella Typhi** (water-borne). **Aspergillus** moulds (aflatoxins in groundnuts and maize).

blocks.title: Useful fermentation
blocks.md: **Lactic acid bacteria** ferment sugars to lactic acid (yoghurt, fermented cassava and cereal foods, pickles). **Yeasts** ferment sugar to ethanol and carbon dioxide (bread, traditional drinks such as palm wine). Controlled fermentation preserves food, improves flavour and can improve digestibility or reduce toxic compounds.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Pathogens are not always visible, smelly or tasty-different.
- Boiling kills growing cells but not all spores or toxins.
- Intoxication needs no live bacteria to remain in the food.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Calculation
blocks.statement: N0 = 200 cells per gram, generation time 40 minutes. Find N after 4 hours.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Low-acid cans
blocks.statement: Why is under-processing of canned low-acid vegetables dangerous?
steps: Spores of Clostridium botulinum may survive and grow in the oxygen-free, low-acid can.
They produce a very potent toxin; correct sterilisation is essential.

lessons.title: Food processing technology
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus (Upper Sixth part) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe smoking, salting, fermentation and extrusion
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Temperatures and times are common textbook values and must be checked; D-value example is illustrative.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Heat processing
blocks.md: **Pasteurisation**: mild heat to destroy pathogens (milk: about 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, or 63 degrees for 30 minutes). **UHT**: about 135 to 150 degrees for a few seconds, then aseptic packing; long shelf life without refrigeration until opened. **Canning (commercial sterilisation)**: food sealed in containers and heated enough to destroy spores (about 121 degrees for low-acid foods). Time and temperature depend on the food, can size and heat penetration. A **D-value** is the time at a given temperature to reduce the population by 90% (one log cycle); for example with D = 2 min, 6 D = 12 min gives a million-fold (6 log) reduction.

blocks.title: Cold and drying
blocks.md: **Refrigeration** (about 0 to 5 degrees Celsius) slows microbial and enzyme action. **Freezing** (around -18 degrees or lower) stops microbial growth; **fast freezing** forms small ice crystals and less drip loss. **Drying** (sun, air, spray, freeze-drying) lowers water activity; sun-drying is cheap but needs protection from dust, insects and rain. **Freeze-drying** keeps quality but costs more.

blocks.caption: A bar chart: with D = 2 minutes the log10 of the surviving cells falls from 6 to 0 over 12 minutes.
blocks.alt: Bar chart of log10 survivors: 6 at 0 minutes, 4 at 4, 2 at 8 and 0 at 12 minutes, with D equal to 2 minutes.

blocks.title: Other methods
blocks.md: **Smoking** (drying, antimicrobial compounds, flavour, often with salt). **Salting/curing** and **sugar**. **Fermentation** (lactic, alcoholic). **Extrusion**: food forced under pressure and heat through a die to make snacks, pasta and texturised proteins. **Irradiation** (approved in some countries) and **high-pressure processing** are other technologies at outline level.

blocks.title: Packaging
blocks.md: Packaging protects from contamination, moisture, oxygen, light and physical damage, gives information (label), and extends shelf life. Types: glass, metal cans, plastics, paper and composites; **modified-atmosphere packaging** replaces air with another gas mixture. Packaging waste must be managed responsibly.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Pasteurised milk is not sterile.
- Freezing is not a kill step.
- A D-value is not a total time: the process must reach many D-values.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - D-value
blocks.statement: A population of 10^6 cells has D = 2 min at a set temperature. How long to reduce it to 10^0 (1 cell)?
steps: Six log cycles are needed (10^6 to 10^0).

blocks.title: Example 2 - Choose a process
blocks.statement: A dairy in Bamenda wants milk to be safe and stay good for a few days in a fridge. Which process is suitable?
steps: Pasteurisation kills pathogens while keeping flavour.
Refrigeration slows growth of surviving organisms.

lessons.title: Food quality, hazards and HACCP
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Food Science and Nutrition syllabus (Upper Sixth part) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Classify hazards: biological, chemical, physical, allergens
Explain good hygiene practice and the seven HACCP principles
Describe quality control and sensory evaluation
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Triangle-test statistics are simplified (no significance table). Critical limits depend on local regulation.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Hazards
blocks.md: **Biological**: bacteria, viruses, parasites, moulds. **Chemical**: pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals, toxins (e.g. aflatoxins), unapproved additives. **Physical**: stones, glass, metal, hair. **Allergens**: foods such as peanuts, eggs, milk, fish, wheat must be controlled and labelled where required. **Good hygiene practice (GHP)** and **good manufacturing practice (GMP)** (clean premises, trained staff, pest control, traceability) form the base.

blocks.title: HACCP principles
blocks.md: 1. Hazard analysis. 2. Determine **critical control points (CCPs)**. 3. Set **critical limits** (e.g. core temperature at least a set value). 4. Monitoring. 5. Corrective actions when a limit is missed. 6. Verification. 7. Documentation and record keeping. HACCP is preventive, process-based and works with prerequisites such as hygiene.

blocks.caption: A table giving an HACCP example for a chicken stew with hazard, CCP, limit, monitoring and action.
blocks.alt: Table: hazard Salmonella, CCP cooking, limit safe core temperature, monitor with a probe, corrective action cook longer.

blocks.title: Quality and sensory evaluation
blocks.md: Quality includes safety, nutrition, appearance, flavour, texture and consistency. **Quality control** checks raw materials, processes and finished products (sampling, testing, records). **Sensory evaluation** uses trained or consumer panels: **difference tests** (triangle test), **ranking**, **rating (hedonic) scales**; use blind coding, neutral conditions and unbiased samples.

blocks.title: Example plan
blocks.md: Product: cooked chicken stew for a canteen. Hazard: Salmonella survival. CCP: cooking. Critical limit: centre of chicken reaches at least the temperature set by local authority (commonly about 70 degrees or equivalent). Monitoring: probe thermometer for each batch. Corrective action: continue cooking. Verification: periodic checks of thermometers. Records: batch temperature log.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A CCP is not any step; it is where control is essential and a measurable limit exists.
- Sensory panels must not see sample labels (bias).
- HACCP does not replace hygiene.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Classify
blocks.statement: Classify: (a) a piece of glass in a jar of jam, (b) aflatoxin in groundnuts, (c) Salmonella in eggs.
steps: (a) is a physical hazard; (b) is a chemical hazard (toxin).

blocks.title: Example 2 - Triangle test
blocks.statement: In a triangle test, three samples are given, two identical. 12 of 20 tasters pick the odd one out correctly. Is this clearly better than guessing (one third would be about 7)?
steps: Guessing would give about 20/3 = 6.7, so 7 correct.
12 is well above this, suggesting a real detectable difference (formal statistics required for a firm conclusion).

exercises.prompt: Design a HACCP summary for fried fish sold at a roadside stall (hazard, CCP, limit, monitoring).
exercises.model: Hazard: bacteria (from raw fish, handling) and cross-contamination. CCP: cooking (core temperature) and cold or hot holding. Limit: fish cooked until hot and firm throughout; hot-holding above about 60 degrees or sold quickly. Monitoring: visual check and thermometer if available; corrective: recook; also clean hands and water.
exercises.rubric: 1 mark each of hazard, CCP, limit, monitoring.
